functional.text: Send a 1:1 message; it is delivered to every device of the recipient.
Group chats of up to 200 members; a group message reaches every member.
History is kept for 1 year and syncs to any device, including a newly signed-in one.
Recipients who are offline get a push notification and catch up when they reconnect.
Secondary: online indicator and read receipts.

non_functional.text: Online-to-online delivery latency < 500 ms at p99 (real-time feel).
A message acknowledged to the sender is never lost, and appears in the same order on every device.
Highly available: losing a server only causes a quick reconnect; ~10M concurrent connections at peak.

assumptions.text: 50M DAU × 40 msgs/day; 20% of DAU connected at peak; peak = 3× average.
~200 B stored per message; media lives in blob storage and messages carry a link.
Average group size ~50 for delivery math; a third of messages go to groups.

out_of_scope.text: End-to-end encryption key management, voice/video calls, the media upload pipeline.

api.notes: client_msg_id makes retries idempotent; the ack means 'persisted'.
Catch-up and history paging, used on reconnect and on a new device.
Tells a reconnecting device which conversations to sync.

api.response: server pushes 'message', 'receipt' and 'presence' frames; client acks by seq

data.name: messages
data.fields: conversation_id (partition key), seq (clustering), message_id, client_msg_id, sender_id, body, created_at
data.why: Append-heavy, read as 'latest N of one conversation': a wide-column store partitioned by conversation fits; ~146 TB/year.

data.name: conversations + conversation_members
data.fields: conversations(conversation_id, type, last_seq); conversation_members(conversation_id, user_id, role, joined_at, last_read_seq)
data.why: Small and relational; read on every fan-out (cached), written on joins and to bump last_seq.

data.name: sessions
data.why: Ephemeral routing state; doubles as presence.

parts.title: Connection tier and routing
parts.problem: Hold ~10M open WebSocket connections across ~170 gateways and, for any message, find the gateway(s) holding the recipient's devices in a few milliseconds.

options.name: Broadcast every message to every gateway (pub/sub)
options.cons: each gateway sees every delivery: >1M deliveries/s × 170 gateways is wasted work

options.name: Place users deterministically: consistent hash user → gateway
options.pros: no lookup; the sender computes the target
options.cons: the load balancer must read auth before routing; a user's devices are forced onto one box; a lost gateway moves many users at once

options.name: Connect anywhere + session registry (device → gateway) with heartbeat TTL
options.pros: any gateway takes any device; the registry doubles as presence
options.cons: one lookup per delivery; stale entries live until the TTL expires

parts.choice: Gateways behind an L4 load balancer + a session registry (device → gateway) in Redis with a heartbeat TTL
parts.why: 10M connections at ~60k per box is ~170 stateful gateways. Keeping state only there (plus a small registry, 10M entries × ~100 B ≈ 1 GB) lets everything else stay stateless; the TTL clears entries of crashed gateways within a minute.

nodes.label: Mobile / web app (one socket per device)

parts.title: Message persistence and ordering
parts.problem: Store ~70k messages/s at peak exactly once, give every message of a conversation an order all devices agree on, and keep a year (~146 TB) readable by conversation.

options.name: Order by client timestamp
options.cons: clocks skew, so two phones show different orders

options.name: One global sequence (SQL auto-increment)
options.cons: a single hot counter at 70k/s and a single point of failure; nobody needs cross-conversation order

options.name: Time-ordered ids (Snowflake)
options.cons: two messages sent in the same millisecond via different servers can swap; gaps are undetectable

options.name: Per-conversation sequence + wide-column store keyed by (conversation_id, seq)
options.pros: order exactly where users see it; scales out by conversation; gaps are detectable
options.cons: one counter per conversation; a very busy group is a hot partition

parts.choice: Per-conversation sequence from an atomic counter, messages stored in Cassandra partitioned by conversation_id and clustered by seq
parts.why: N2 needs one order per conversation, not a global one. INCR on a per-conversation key is O(1) and spreads across Redis shards; the store's access pattern is 'latest N of conversation X', which a partition + clustering key answers in one read. client_msg_id makes retried sends idempotent.

parts.title: Offline delivery, push and catch-up
parts.problem: A recipient's device has no open connection: it must learn that something arrived, and on reconnect (or on a brand-new device) fetch exactly what it missed.

options.name: Per-device inbox queue (copy each message until the device acks)
options.cons: storage and writes multiply by devices; a lost phone's queue grows forever

options.name: Put the message itself in the push payload
options.cons: push is best effort with tiny payload limits; it is not history and can't fill gaps

options.name: Push as a wake-up hint + cursor sync (device keeps last_seq per conversation, pulls after_seq)
options.pros: one stored copy; works for any number of devices and for new devices
options.cons: the client must track cursors and page; one extra round trip on reconnect

parts.choice: Push (APNs/FCM) only as a wake-up hint; devices catch up by pulling after their last seq per conversation
parts.why: Messages are already stored once in order (P2), so a cursor is enough to catch up; conversations.last_seq tells a device which conversations changed. Push providers are best effort, so they carry no data we depend on.

parts.title: Group fan-out
parts.problem: A third of messages go to groups of up to 200 people; peak deliveries exceed 1M/s. The sender's acknowledgement must not wait for 200 recipients.

options.name: Sender's chat server delivers to each member inline
options.cons: ack latency grows with group size; one slow gateway stalls the sender

options.name: Fan-out on write: copy the message into every member's inbox table
options.pros: a member's reads are one query
options.cons: 200 writes per group message (~10M writes/s at peak) for data already stored once

options.name: Persist once, publish to a stream; async fan-out workers deliver
options.pros: sender acked after one write; workers retry independently and scale with partitions
options.cons: one more hop (tens of ms); at-least-once delivery means clients must dedup

parts.choice: Persist once, publish to a Kafka stream keyed by conversation; fan-out workers resolve members and gateways and deliver
parts.why: Deliveries (>1M/s) are ~20× the send rate, so they need their own tier that can lag and retry without touching the sender's < 500 ms ack. Keying the stream by conversation keeps per-conversation order through fan-out.

deep_dives.title: Server-to-client transport

options.name: short polling
options.cons: 10M clients × 1 req/s, mostly empty, and up to 1 s late

options.name: long polling
options.cons: a new request after every message; awkward for sends

options.name: WebSocket
options.pros: one bidirectional connection per device; server pushes instantly
options.cons: stateful servers that need a routing registry

deep_dives.choice: WebSocket, with long polling as a fallback for hostile networks
deep_dives.why: N1 needs the server to speak first; 10M concurrent connections fit on ~170 gateways and the statefulness is isolated in that tier (P1).

deep_dives.title: Retries, duplicates and gaps

options.name: exactly-once delivery end to end
options.cons: needs distributed transactions across gateways and phones

options.name: at-least-once + dedup by client_msg_id and seq
options.cons: clients must drop duplicates and fetch gaps

deep_dives.choice: at-least-once delivery with dedup: the store ignores a repeated client_msg_id, clients drop a seq they already have and fetch any gap
deep_dives.why: N2: the sender retries until it gets an ack, workers redeliver after a crash, and phones reconnect mid-stream. Sequence numbers make both duplicates and gaps visible, so order stays identical on every device.

deep_dives.title: Gateway crash and reconnect storms

options.name: clients reconnect immediately
options.cons: 60k clients hit the load balancer in the same second

options.name: exponential backoff with jitter, then sync after last_seq
options.cons: a few seconds of extra delay

deep_dives.choice: exponential backoff with jitter; the registry entry expires by TTL; the device syncs after its last seq
deep_dives.why: N3: a gateway loss must cost only a reconnect. Jitter turns a thundering herd into a smooth ramp, and cursor sync means nothing is lost while the device was away.

deep_dives.title: Presence and read receipts

options.name: push every presence change to all contacts
options.cons: presence churn would dwarf message traffic

options.name: presence from the registry, fetched when a chat opens; receipts as small messages in the conversation
options.cons: presence can be a heartbeat interval stale

deep_dives.choice: presence read from the session registry on demand; read receipts update last_read_seq and travel as lightweight messages
deep_dives.why: F5 is secondary; it must not multiply load. A receipt is just 'read up to seq', which one number per member captures.

wrapup.bottlenecks: Very active large groups (fan-out cost and a hot conversation partition), the session registry on every delivery (shard by device, cache locally), the per-conversation counter of a busy group.
wrapup.failures: Gateway crash: clients reconnect with backoff + jitter and sync from last seq. Fan-out worker lag or crash: Kafka retains messages and workers replay from their offset; duplicates are dropped by seq. Retried sends are deduped by client_msg_id. Push provider down: devices still catch up on next open.
wrapup.monitoring: End-to-end delivery latency (send → device ack) p99, connections per gateway, reconnect rate, Kafka consumer lag, registry hit rate, push failure rate.
wrapup.scale: More gateways behind the LB; shard the registry by device; add stream partitions and Cassandra nodes; for very large groups (thousands) switch to pull-on-open instead of per-member fan-out.
wrapup.future: End-to-end encryption, message search, multi-region with a home region per conversation.
